decks.title: Trial Balance and Rectification of Errors — Part 1: Preparing the Trial Balance
goals: State the meaning and the objectives of a trial balance and the side on which each kind of account is shown
Prepare a trial balance by the balances method and describe the totals method and the totals and balances method
Explain why an agreed trial balance does not prove that the books are free from errors

slides.heading: The trial balance: checking the ledger
slides.body_md: Part 1: the **trial balance**: meaning, objectives, preparation and limitations.

visual.alt: Flow: journal entries are posted, ledger accounts are balanced, the trial balance is prepared, and the financial statements follow
visual.caption: Where the trial balance sits in the accounting process.

slides.narration: After transactions are journalised, posted and balanced, a business lists the balances of all its ledger accounts in a statement called the trial balance. In this part we learn what it is, what it is for, how to prepare it by the balances method, and why an agreed trial balance still cannot prove that the books are free from errors. We work with imagined firms, Kabir Traders and Naina Stores.

slides.heading: What is a trial balance?

rows: A statement of the debit balances and the credit balances of the ledger accounts
On a given date, usually the last day of the accounting period
The balances of the ledger accounts after posting and balancing
Whether the debit total equals the credit total, that is, arithmetical accuracy

visual.alt: Table on the meaning of a trial balance: what it is, when it is drawn up, what it is built from and what it tests

slides.narration: A trial balance is a statement of the debit balances and the credit balances of the ledger accounts on a given date. It is drawn up after posting and balancing, usually at the end of the accounting period. If every posting was arithmetically correct, the two columns total the same. If they differ, an error exists somewhere in the books.

slides.heading: Objectives of a trial balance

rows: Equal column totals show that posting and balancing are arithmetically sound
A difference warns that an error exists and narrows the search
All the balances appear in one statement
Help to prepare the financial statements
Its figures feed the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet

visual.alt: Table of the four objectives of a trial balance and how each helps

slides.narration: There are four objectives. First, it checks the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger. Second, a difference between the columns warns that an error exists and helps to locate it. Third, it summarises all the ledger balances in one statement. Fourth, it supplies the figures from which the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet are prepared.

slides.heading: Which side does each account take?

rows: Assets such as cash, bank, furniture and machinery
Liabilities such as creditors and loans
Expenses and losses such as purchases, wages and rent
Revenues and gains such as sales and commission received
Provisions, for example for doubtful debts

visual.alt: Table of what appears in the debit column and the credit column of a trial balance: assets, expenses, drawings, debtors and opening stock on the debit side; liabilities, revenues, capital, creditors and provisions on the credit side

slides.narration: Look at the table. Assets, expenses and losses, drawings, debtors and opening stock carry debit balances, so they go in the debit column. Liabilities, capital, revenues and gains, creditors and provisions carry credit balances, so they go in the credit column. The column depends on the nature of the balance, never on its size.

slides.heading: Quick check: which column?
slides.body_md: Decide the column in which the drawings balance of an imagined firm is shown.
slides.narration: Drawings are what the proprietor withdraws from the business. Decide whether the balance of the drawings account is a debit or a credit, and remember that the column depends on the nature of the balance.

slides.heading: Three methods of preparing a trial balance
slides.body_md: The **balances method** is the one used in practice and in examinations. The other two methods are described here.

rows: Only the closing balance of each account, in the debit or credit column
The two columns of balances agree
The total of each side of every account
The two columns of totals agree
Both the totals and the balances

visual.alt: Table of the three methods of preparing a trial balance: balances method, totals method, and totals and balances method

slides.narration: There are three methods. In the balances method only the closing balance of each account is listed. In the totals method the total of each side of every account is listed. In the totals and balances method both are shown. In each case the two columns must agree. The balances method is the one we use to prepare a trial balance.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: totals and balances of Naina Stores
slides.body_md: Six transactions of **Naina Stores**, an imagined shop, are posted. Totals: each column **₹3,00,000**; balances: each column **₹1,90,000**.
bullets: The totals method uses the first two columns of figures.
The balances method uses the last two columns of figures.
Verma Traders: debit total less than credit total, so a credit balance.

visual.alt: Totals and balances of the six accounts of Naina Stores: total debits and total credits each 3,00,000 rupees, debit balances and credit balances each 1,90,000 rupees

slides.narration: Naina Stores, an imagined shop, posts six transactions. By the totals method, the debit totals and the credit totals each come to rupees three lakh. By the balances method, the debit balances of cash, purchases and wages, and the credit balances of capital, sales and the supplier, each come to rupees one lakh ninety thousand. Both methods agree, but only the balances method is needed for the trial balance.

slides.heading: Steps in preparing a trial balance

rows: Post all the journal entries and balance every ledger account
Write the heading with the name of the firm and the date
List each account with its balance in the debit column or the credit column according to its nature
Compare the totals; if they differ, look for the error before going further

visual.alt: Table of the five steps of preparing a trial balance by the balances method

slides.narration: First, post the journal entries and balance every ledger account. Then write the heading with the name of the firm and the date. List each account with its balance in the debit column or the credit column according to its nature. Total the two columns and compare them. If the totals differ, look for the error before going further.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: trial balance of Kabir Traders
slides.body_md: **Kabir Traders**, an imagined firm, lists sixteen balances on 31 March 2028. Each column totals **₹8,72,000**.
bullets: Assets, expenses and drawings are in the debit column.
Capital, liabilities and incomes are in the credit column.

visual.alt: Trial balance of Kabir Traders on 31 March 2028: sixteen accounts, debit column and credit column each totalling 8,72,000 rupees

slides.narration: Kabir Traders, an imagined firm, lists sixteen balances on the last day of March. The debit column holds cash, debtors, stock, furniture, machinery, purchases, wages, rent, carriage inwards and drawings. The credit column holds capital, creditors, sales, discount received and the bank loan. Each column totals rupees eight lakh seventy two thousand, so the trial balance agrees.

slides.heading: Quick check: the missing balance
slides.body_md: Find the capital that makes the columns of an imagined trial balance agree.
slides.narration: Add the debit balances. Then add the credit balances that are known. The missing credit balance is the amount that makes the credit column equal the debit column.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: choosing the column
slides.body_md: Decide the nature of each balance, and then the column, for eight accounts of Kabir Traders.

visual.alt: Table giving the nature and the trial balance column of eight accounts of Kabir Traders: carriage inwards debit, discount received credit, bank loan credit, plant and machinery debit, debtors debit, capital credit, creditors credit and opening stock debit

slides.narration: Name the nature of the account first. Carriage inwards is an expense, so it is a debit. Discount received is an income, so it is a credit. The bank loan is a liability, a credit. Machinery, debtors and stock are assets, debits. Capital is the owner's claim, a credit, and creditors are a liability, a credit.

slides.heading: When the columns do not agree

rows: The difference equals the balance of one account
That balance may have been left out of the trial balance, or listed only once
The difference is divisible by nine
Two digits of an amount may have been transposed, for example 63 written as 36
The difference is twice an amount
A balance may have been written in the wrong column
The difference is a round figure
A total or a balance may have been wrongly added or carried forward

visual.alt: Table of clues when the columns of a trial balance do not agree: a difference equal to one balance, divisible by nine, twice an amount, or a round figure, with what each may mean

slides.narration: If the columns differ, do not force them to agree. Look at the difference. If it equals one balance, that balance may have been left out. If it divides by nine, two digits may have been transposed. If it is twice an amount, a balance may be in the wrong column. A round difference suggests a wrong total or a wrong carry forward.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: Tara Footwear's columns
slides.body_md: Before its errors are found, the trial balance of **Tara Footwear**, an imagined firm, shows columns that differ by **₹3,600**.
bullets: The debit column is higher, so the credit side needs the difference.
The difference divides by nine, a clue to transposed digits.

headers: Tara Footwear: trial balance before the errors are found
rows: Suspense A/c to make the columns agree

visual.alt: Trial balance totals of Tara Footwear: debit column 9,35,700 rupees and credit column 9,32,100 rupees; the difference of 3,600 rupees is carried to the credit side of a Suspense A/c

slides.narration: Tara Footwear, an imagined firm, totals its trial balance. The debit column is rupees nine lakh thirty five thousand seven hundred and the credit column is rupees nine lakh thirty two thousand one hundred. The debit column is higher by rupees three thousand six hundred, so the difference is carried to the credit side of a suspense account, which we meet in the next part. The difference divides by nine, which is one clue to the error.

slides.heading: What an agreed trial balance does not show

rows: Both debit and credit are missing
Goods of ₹9,000 sold on credit to Anand Pillai were not entered in any book.
The same amount is debited and credited, to the wrong kind of account
A computer bought for ₹25,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c.
Wrong account of the same kind
The amount is on the right side of a wrong account
Commission of ₹5,400 received by cheque was credited to Rent A/c.
Wages A/c was overcast by ₹2,000 and Salaries A/c was undercast by ₹2,000.

visual.alt: Table of errors that can remain in the books although the trial balance agrees: complete omission, error of principle, wrong account of the same kind, and compensating errors, each with why the columns agree and an imagined example

slides.narration: Agreement of the columns shows only that debits equal credits in total. A complete omission leaves both sides out. An error of principle puts the same amount on both sides, but in the wrong kind of account. A wrong account of the same kind keeps the totals. Compensating errors cancel each other. So an agreed trial balance does not prove that the books are free from errors.

slides.heading: Quick check: does agreement prove accuracy?
slides.body_md: True or false: an agreed trial balance proves that the ledger is free from errors.
slides.narration: Think about the errors that put the same amount on both sides, or leave out both sides of a transaction. Would the columns still agree in those cases?

slides.heading: From trial balance to final accounts

rows: Opening stock, purchases, carriage inwards, sales and wages
Trading account, to find the gross profit
Profit and loss account, to find the net profit
Capital, drawings, bank loan, creditors, debtors, furniture, machinery, cash and bank

visual.alt: Table showing where the balances of the Kabir Traders trial balance are used: trading account, profit and loss account and balance sheet

slides.narration: The trial balance is the starting point of the financial statements. Opening stock, purchases, carriage inwards, sales and wages go to the trading account. Rent and discount received go to the profit and loss account. Capital, drawings, the loan, creditors, debtors and the other assets go to the balance sheet. Preparing these statements is the subject of a later chapter.

slides.heading: Quick check: order of the steps
slides.body_md: Arrange the steps of preparing a trial balance by the balances method.
slides.narration: Think about what must be finished before the balances can be listed, and what is done last, after both columns are written.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1
bullets: A trial balance lists debit and credit balances on a date to test arithmetical accuracy.
Assets, expenses, drawings and debtors are debits; liabilities, capital, revenues, creditors and provisions are credits.
An agreed trial balance does not prove that the books are free from errors.

rows: Debit and credit balances of ledger accounts on a date, to test arithmetical accuracy
Check accuracy, locate errors, summarise the ledger, help prepare financial statements
Assets, expenses, drawings and debtors on the debit side; liabilities, capital, revenues, creditors and provisions on the credit side
Balances, totals, and totals and balances
An agreed trial balance does not prove the books are free from errors

visual.alt: Summary table of the trial balance: meaning, objectives, sides, methods and the limit

slides.narration: To sum up. A trial balance lists the debit and credit balances of the ledger on a date, to test arithmetical accuracy. Its objectives are to check accuracy, to help locate errors, to summarise the ledger and to supply figures for the financial statements. Assets, expenses, drawings and debtors are debits. Liabilities, capital, revenues, creditors and provisions are credits. An agreed trial balance does not prove the books are free from errors.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Heading with the name and the date; two columns.
Place each balance by its nature and total both columns.
Never say that an agreed trial balance proves accuracy.

rows: Write the heading with the name of the firm and the date
It is part of the standard format
Place every balance by its nature, not by its size
Assets and expenses are debits, liabilities and incomes are credits
Total both columns and state whether they agree
Do not write that an agreed trial balance proves accuracy
Several errors do not affect it

visual.alt: Exam tips table for the trial balance

slides.narration: In the examination, write the heading with the name of the firm and the date, and use two columns. Place every balance by its nature, assets and expenses on the debit side, liabilities and incomes on the credit side. Total both columns and say whether they agree. Never write that an agreed trial balance proves that the books are accurate, because several errors do not affect it.

visual.caption: Four types of errors, and which of them disturb the trial balance.

slides.narration: Even a careful accountant makes mistakes. In this part we sort errors into four types, find out which of them disturb the trial balance, and learn how to correct them, before the trial balance is prepared and after it. We use a suspense account for the difference and see it close. Finally, we find the effect of each error on net profit. We work with imagined firms, Ritu Garments and Tara Footwear.

slides.heading: One-sided and two-sided errors
slides.body_md: An error is **one-sided** when the two sides of the entries carry unequal amounts, and **two-sided** when both sides are affected equally.

rows: Only one side of an entry is affected, so the two sides carry unequal amounts
Both sides are affected equally, or the whole transaction is left out

visual.alt: Table of one-sided errors, which make the trial balance disagree, and two-sided errors, which leave it in agreement

slides.narration: Errors can be grouped by their effect on the trial balance. A one-sided error affects only one side of an entry, so the debits and credits become unequal and the trial balance disagrees. A two-sided error affects both sides equally, or leaves out the whole transaction, so the trial balance still agrees. This is the grouping that decides how the error is found and corrected.

slides.heading: Errors of commission

rows: Rent of ₹4,500 paid in cash posted to Rent A/c as ₹5,400
A receipt of ₹2,000 from a debtor posted to the debit side of his account instead of the credit side
Cash of ₹2,000 received from Rohit Sen credited to the account of Devika Nair
The August sales book total of ₹60,000 was posted to Sales A/c as ₹64,000; the debtors' accounts were posted correctly.
Purchases A/c balanced as ₹1,24,000 instead of ₹1,42,000
A page total of ₹8,400 carried to the next page as ₹4,800

visual.alt: Table of errors of commission: wrong amount, wrong side, wrong account, wrong totalling, wrong balancing and wrong carrying forward, each with an imagined example and whether the trial balance agrees

slides.narration: An error of commission is a wrong posting or a wrong calculation. The amount, the side or the account may be wrong. A book may be wrongly totalled, an account wrongly balanced, or a total wrongly carried forward. A wrong amount, a wrong side and a wrong total put unequal amounts on the two sides, so the trial balance disagrees. Posting to a wrong account does not.

slides.heading: Errors of omission

rows: Complete: the whole transaction is left out
Goods of ₹9,000 sold on credit to Anand Pillai were not entered in any book.
Partial: only one side is posted
A credit purchase of ₹6,000 from Mehta Cloth House was credited to Mehta Cloth House but not debited to Purchases A/c.

visual.alt: Table of errors of omission: complete omission, which leaves the trial balance in agreement, and partial omission, which makes it disagree, each with an imagined example

slides.narration: An error of omission means that a transaction is left out. In a complete omission, the whole transaction is missing from the books, so debits and credits stay equal and the trial balance agrees. In a partial omission, only one side is posted, so the trial balance disagrees.

slides.heading: Errors of principle and compensating errors

rows: A capital item treated as a revenue item, or the reverse; the entry balances
Furniture bought for ₹15,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c.
Errors whose effects on the two sides cancel
Wages A/c was overcast by ₹2,000 and Salaries A/c was undercast by ₹2,000.

visual.alt: Table of errors of principle and compensating errors, each with meaning, an imagined example and the effect on the trial balance

slides.narration: An error of principle treats a capital item as a revenue item, or the reverse. Furniture debited to purchases is an example. The entry balances, so the trial balance agrees. Compensating errors are two or more errors whose effects cancel. Wages overcast by two thousand and salaries undercast by two thousand are an example. The trial balance agrees, though both accounts are wrong.

slides.heading: Quick check: name the error
slides.body_md: Classify an imagined firm's error in which the cost of installing a machine was charged to wages.
slides.narration: Decide whether the cost of installing a machine is a capital item or a revenue item. Then decide what kind of error arises when it is debited to an expense account.

visual.caption: Only one-sided errors disturb the trial balance.

slides.narration: Ask one question. Does the error put unequal amounts on the two sides? If yes, it is a one-sided error and the trial balance disagrees. If no, it is a two-sided error and the trial balance still agrees, so the error is found only by checking the books. The question decides whether a difference appears in the trial balance at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: classify the errors of Ritu Garments
slides.body_md: **Ritu Garments**, an imagined firm in the imagined town of Ranipur, finds six errors after its trial balance. Each is classified.
bullets: Errors 1, 2 and 3 are one-sided.
Errors 4, 5 and 6 are two-sided.

rows: The August sales book total of ₹60,000 was posted to Sales A/c as ₹64,000; the debtors' accounts were posted correctly.
A credit purchase of ₹6,000 from Mehta Cloth House was credited to Mehta Cloth House but not debited to Purchases A/c.
Rent of ₹4,500 paid in cash was posted to Rent A/c as ₹5,400.
A credit sale of ₹8,000 to Kiran Rao was not recorded in any book.
Furniture bought for ₹15,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c.
Wages A/c was overcast by ₹2,000 and Salaries A/c was undercast by ₹2,000.

visual.alt: Classification of the six errors of Ritu Garments by type, effect on the trial balance and effect on net profit: errors 1 to 3 are one-sided and make the trial balance disagree; errors 4 to 6 are two-sided and leave it in agreement

slides.narration: Ritu Garments, an imagined firm, finds six errors. The sales book total, the missing debit to purchases, and the rent posted too high are one-sided, so the trial balance disagrees. The omitted credit sale, the furniture debited to purchases, and the wages and salaries errors are two-sided, so the trial balance still agrees. The last column shows the effect on net profit, which we use later.

visual.caption: Rectification before and after the trial balance.

slides.narration: Look at the flow. If an error is found before the trial balance is prepared, a one-sided error is corrected by an explanatory entry in the account, and a two-sided error by a journal entry. If it is found after the trial balance, the difference is placed in a suspense account so that the columns agree, and each error is then corrected by a journal entry until the suspense account closes.

slides.heading: Rectification before the trial balance

headers: How it is rectified before the trial balance
rows: An explanatory entry on the proper side of the affected account
A cash sale of ₹7,200 was entered correctly in the cash book but posted to Sales A/c as ₹2,700.
A journal entry debiting and crediting the accounts concerned
A computer bought for ₹25,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c.

visual.alt: Table of rectification before the trial balance: explanatory entry in the account for a one-sided error and a journal entry for a two-sided error

slides.narration: Before the trial balance is prepared, no difference exists, so no suspense account is needed. A one-sided error is corrected in the affected account itself, with an explanatory entry on the proper side. A two-sided error is corrected by a journal entry that debits and credits the accounts concerned, so that the right accounts carry the right amounts.

slides.narration: A suspense account is a temporary account for the difference between the columns of a trial balance. If the credit column is higher, the account is debited, and the other way round. Each time a one-sided error is found, the suspense account is debited or credited to correct it. Here the account of Ritu Garments opens with rupees nine thousand one hundred and closes with nothing, because both sides total rupees ten thousand.

slides.heading: Rectification after the trial balance

rows: Total the two columns of the trial balance and find the difference
Place the difference in the Suspense A/c, on the side with the lower total
For each one-sided error found, pass a journal entry with the Suspense A/c as one of its accounts
Correct each two-sided error by a journal entry without the Suspense A/c
Post to the Suspense A/c; when every error is found its balance is nil

visual.alt: Table of the five steps of rectification after the trial balance with a Suspense A/c

slides.narration: After the trial balance is prepared, first find the difference and place it in the suspense account on the side with the lower total. For each one-sided error found, pass a journal entry in which the suspense account is one of the accounts. A two-sided error is corrected without the suspense account. When every error has been found, the suspense account has a nil balance.

slides.body_md: Find the amount carried to the suspense account for an imagined firm with two one-sided errors.
slides.narration: For each one-sided error decide whether it makes the debit side or the credit side higher. Combine the two effects. The net difference is the amount of the suspense account.

slides.heading: Effect of errors on net profit

rows: Expense overstated: a capital item debited to an expense, or an expense charged twice
Expense understated: a revenue item debited to a capital account, or an expense left out
Income understated: a sale or an income left out
Income overstated: a sale or an income recorded twice or too high
Equal amounts moved between two expenses, or between two incomes
Only assets, liabilities, capital or drawings are wrongly posted

visual.alt: Table of the effect on net profit of wrongly treated items: expense overstated understates profit, expense understated overstates profit, income left out understates profit, income overstated overstates profit, equal amounts moved between expenses or incomes have no effect, and errors in balance sheet accounts alone have no effect

slides.narration: An error changes net profit only if it affects an expense or an income account by an unequal amount. If an expense is overstated, profit is understated. If an expense is understated, profit is overstated. A sale left out understates profit. Equal amounts moved between two expenses, or between two incomes, have no effect. Errors in assets, liabilities, capital or drawings alone do not change profit.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning and objectives of a trial balance
sections.body_md:
A **trial balance** is a statement of the debit balances and the credit balances of all ledger accounts on a given date, prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of posting and balancing. It is drawn up after the ledger accounts are balanced, usually on the last day of the accounting period.

**Objectives:** (1) to check arithmetical accuracy; (2) to help locate errors, since a difference shows that an error exists; (3) to summarise the ledger accounts in one statement; (4) to provide the figures from which the financial statements are prepared.

key_terms.definition_md: A statement of the debit and credit balances of ledger accounts on a given date, prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of the books.
The balance of an account whose debit side is larger; it arises for assets, expenses, drawings and debtors.
The balance of an account whose credit side is larger; it arises for liabilities, capital, revenues, creditors and provisions.

sections.heading: 2. Which side each account takes
sections.body_md: In the trial balance, **assets, expenses and losses, drawings and debtors** (and opening stock) are shown on the **debit** side. **Liabilities, capital, revenues and gains, creditors and provisions** are shown on the **credit** side. The side is fixed by the nature of the balance, not by its size.

sections.heading: 3. Preparing a trial balance
sections.body_md:
There are three methods. In the **balances method** only the closing balance of each ledger account is listed in the debit or credit column; this is the usual method. In the **totals method** the total of the debit side and of the credit side of each account is listed. In the **totals and balances method** both are shown.

**Steps (balances method):** post the journal and balance every account; write the heading with the name and date; list each balance in its column; total both columns; compare the totals.

A method of preparing a trial balance by listing the total of each side of every ledger account.
A method of preparing a trial balance that shows both the totals and the balances of the ledger accounts.

sections.heading: 4. When the columns differ, and limitations
sections.body_md:
If the two columns differ, an error exists. Useful clues: a difference equal to one balance (a balance omitted or listed once); a difference divisible by nine (transposed digits); a difference equal to twice an amount (a balance written in the wrong column).

**Limitations.** An agreed trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy. The books may still contain a **complete omission**, an **error of principle**, a posting to a **wrong account of the same kind**, and **compensating errors**, none of which changes either column. It is therefore not conclusive proof of accuracy.

sections.heading: 5. Types of errors
sections.body_md:
**Errors of commission:** a wrong posting (wrong amount, side or account) or a wrong calculation (wrong totalling, balancing or carrying forward). **Errors of omission:** a transaction left out completely (complete omission) or only one side posted (partial omission). **Errors of principle:** a capital item treated as a revenue item, or the reverse. **Compensating errors:** two or more errors whose effects cancel.

An error is **one-sided** if it puts unequal amounts on the two sides (the trial balance disagrees) and **two-sided** if it does not (the trial balance agrees). A wrong amount, a wrong side, a wrong total and a partial omission are one-sided; a complete omission, an error of principle, a wrong account and compensating errors are two-sided.

key_terms.definition_md: A mistake in posting or calculation in which a transaction is recorded but with a wrong amount, side or account, or a book is wrongly totalled, balanced or carried forward.
A mistake in which a transaction is left out of the books completely, or only one side of it is posted.
A mistake in which a capital item is treated as a revenue item, or the reverse, against accounting principles.
Two or more errors whose effects on the debit and credit sides cancel each other.
Spending that gives a benefit lasting more than one accounting period, such as the purchase of furniture or machinery.
Spending whose benefit is used up within the accounting period, such as wages, rent and repairs.

sections.heading: 7. Suspense account, rectification after the trial balance, and effect on profit
sections.body_md:
If the trial balance is prepared and does not agree, the difference is placed in a **suspense account**: on the debit side if the credit column is higher, on the credit side if the debit column is higher. Each **one-sided** error found later is corrected by a journal entry in which the Suspense A/c is one of the accounts; each **two-sided** error is corrected by a journal entry without it. When every error is found, the Suspense A/c closes with a nil balance.

**Effect on net profit:** an error changes profit only if an expense or an income account carries an unequal amount. Expense overstated or income understated: profit understated. Expense understated or income overstated: profit overstated. Equal amounts moved between two expenses or two incomes, or errors in balance sheet accounts alone: no effect. Corrected net profit = reported profit minus the amount by which profit was overstated plus the amount by which it was understated.

An error that affects both sides equally, or leaves out a whole transaction, so the trial balance still agrees.
The excess of revenues over expenses for an accounting period, which increases the capital of the proprietor.

questions.stem_md: Rina Optics, an imagined shop in the imagined town of Ranipur, lists the balances of all its ledger accounts in two columns on 31 March 2028 to test the arithmetical accuracy of its posting. This list is called a

options.text_md: balance sheet
trial balance
profit and loss account
bank reconciliation statement

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** trial balance. A statement of the debit and credit balances of the ledger accounts on a date, drawn up to check arithmetical accuracy, is a trial balance. A balance sheet shows assets and liabilities, a profit and loss account shows income and expenses, and a bank reconciliation statement compares the cash book with the pass book.

questions.stem_md: Anwar Cycles, an imagined dealer, prepares a trial balance every year. Which of the following is NOT an objective of preparing it?

options.text_md: To check the arithmetical accuracy of the ledger accounts
To bring the balances of all ledger accounts together in one statement
To supply the figures from which the financial statements are prepared
To prove that the ledger accounts contain no errors of any kind

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** To prove that the ledger accounts contain no errors of any kind. An agreed trial balance cannot prove that no error exists, because some errors leave both columns equal, so this is not an objective. The other three are genuine objectives: checking accuracy, summarising the balances and supplying figures for the final accounts.

questions.stem_md: Kabir Traders, an imagined firm, has a Drawings A/c with a balance of ₹25,000 on 31 March 2028. In its trial balance this balance is shown on the

options.text_md: debit side
credit side
credit side, since drawings reduce capital
either side, as the proprietor chooses

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debit side. Drawings are withdrawals by the proprietor and carry a debit balance, so they go in the debit column. The fact that drawings reduce capital does not move them to the credit column, and the side is fixed by the nature of the balance, not by choice.

questions.stem_md: Pooja Medicals, an imagined chemist, has a Provision for Doubtful Debts A/c with a balance of ₹4,000 and a Debtors A/c with a balance of ₹52,000. In the trial balance these two balances are placed in the

options.text_md: debit column and the credit column respectively
debit column both
credit column and the debit column respectively
credit column both

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** credit column and the debit column respectively. A provision is a credit balance like a liability, while debtors are an asset with a debit balance. So the provision goes in the credit column and debtors in the debit column.

questions.stem_md: Noor Bakery, an imagined bakery in the imagined town of Chandpur, lists these balances for its trial balance: Wages ₹9,000, Machinery ₹60,000, Drawings ₹7,000 and Interest Received ₹1,800. Which one is placed in the credit column?

Machinery
Interest Received
Drawings

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Interest Received. Interest received is an income, and incomes have credit balances. Wages are an expense, machinery an asset and drawings a withdrawal, and all three have debit balances.

totals method
totals and balances method
journal method

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** balances method. Listing only the closing balances is the balances method. The totals method lists the total of each side of every account, and the totals and balances method shows both. There is no journal method of preparing a trial balance.

credit column with ₹2,250
debit column with ₹2,250
credit column with ₹4,500

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** credit column with ₹4,500. The debit column is larger by ₹4,500, so the credit column needs ₹4,500 more. questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** financial statements. The trial balance summarises the balances from which the trading and profit and loss account and the balance sheet are drawn up. commission
principle
compensation

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** commission. Posting to a wrong account is an error of commission. Nothing is left out, so it is not an omission, no capital or revenue treatment is misjudged, so it is not an error of principle, and no second error cancels it.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** complete omission. A transaction left out of the books altogether is an error of complete omission. Commission means a wrong posting, principle means a wrong capital or revenue treatment, and compensating errors cancel each other.

principle

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** principle. An almirah is a capital item that should be debited to a furniture account; debiting it to Purchases treats it as a revenue item, which is an error of principle. The amount and the accounts are posted, so it is neither an omission nor a commission.

questions.stem_md: Which of these is a compensating error in the books of Umesh Traders, an imagined firm?

options.text_md: Purchases A/c overcast by ₹1,500 only
A sale of ₹1,500 left out of every book
Furniture bought for ₹1,500 debited to Purchases A/c
Purchases A/c overcast by ₹1,500 and Sales A/c overcast by ₹1,500

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Purchases A/c overcast by ₹1,500 and Sales A/c overcast by ₹1,500. Overcasting Purchases adds ₹1,500 to the debit side and overcasting Sales adds ₹1,500 to the credit side, so the two cancel. The second error stands alone, the third is a complete omission and the fourth is an error of principle.

questions.stem_md: Wages of ₹6,000 paid for installing a new machine of Zoya Mills, an imagined firm, were debited to Wages A/c. This is

options.text_md: an error of commission, as a wrong amount was posted
an error of complete omission, as no entry was made
an error of principle, as a capital expense was treated as a revenue expense
a compensating error, as another error cancels it

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** an error of principle, as a capital expense was treated as a revenue expense. Installation cost is part of the cost of the machine, a capital item, so debiting it to Wages treats it as a revenue expense. The right amount and the right side were used, nothing was left out and no second error offsets it.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following errors in the books of Vikram Cycles, an imagined firm, will NOT be disclosed by the trial balance?

options.text_md: Cash of ₹2,500 received was debited to the cash book as ₹2,500 and credited to the debtor as ₹2,050
Goods of ₹3,000 sold on credit to Imran Shaikh were entered in the sales book but posted neither to Sales A/c nor to his account
The purchases book was overcast by ₹800
A payment of ₹1,800 to a creditor was debited to his account but not credited to the cash book

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Goods of ₹3,000 sold on credit to Imran Shaikh were entered in the sales book but posted neither to Sales A/c nor to his account. When both the debit and the credit posting are left out, the columns stay equal, so the trial balance agrees. In the other three, one side carries a different amount from the other, and the columns would differ.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Ganesh Stores, an imagined firm, shows a debit total of ₹6,18,400 and a credit total of ₹6,24,000. The difference is carried to a Suspense A/c, which is shown on the

options.text_md: debit side with ₹5,600
credit side with ₹5,600
debit side with ₹2,800
neither side, because no account is opened until the errors are found

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** debit side with ₹5,600. The credit column is larger by ₹5,600, so the debit column needs ₹5,600 more: the Suspense A/c carries a debit balance of ₹5,600. A credit entry would widen the gap, half the difference has no basis, and the account is opened precisely so that the trial balance agrees while the search goes on.

questions.stem_md: After every error of an imagined firm has been found and rectified, its Suspense A/c will show

options.text_md: a debit balance equal to the original difference
no balance, because the account closes
a credit balance equal to the original difference
a balance equal to half the original difference

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** no balance, because the account closes. The suspense account was opened for the net effect of the one-sided errors, and rectifying each of them brings it back to nil. A balance left over means some error has not been found.

questions.stem_md: After its trial balance was prepared and the difference was placed in a Suspense A/c, Mala Gifts, an imagined shop, found that the purchases book had been overcast by ₹3,000 while the creditors were posted correctly. The rectifying entry is

options.text_md: Purchases A/c Dr. ₹3,000 To Suspense A/c
Suspense A/c Dr. ₹3,000 To Pillai Paper A/c
Pillai Paper A/c Dr. ₹3,000 To Purchases A/c
Suspense A/c Dr. ₹3,000 To Purchases A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Suspense A/c Dr. ₹3,000 To Purchases A/c. The Purchases A/c carries ₹3,000 too much on its debit side, so it is credited to remove the excess. Only one side was wrong, so the other side of the entry is the Suspense A/c: it was credited with the difference when the trial balance was made to agree, and it is debited now to clear that credit. Debiting Purchases would repeat the error, and the creditors were posted correctly.

questions.stem_md: Nikhil Garments, an imagined firm, paid wages of ₹9,500 in cash and debited the amount to Salaries A/c. The rectifying entry is

options.text_md: Wages A/c Dr. ₹9,500 To Salaries A/c
Salaries A/c Dr. ₹9,500 To Wages A/c
Wages A/c Dr. ₹9,500 To Cash A/c
Suspense A/c Dr. ₹9,500 To Salaries A/c

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Wages A/c Dr. ₹9,500 To Salaries A/c. Wages should have been debited and Salaries were debited instead, so Wages is debited and Salaries is credited to cancel the wrong debit. The reverse entry would double the error, cash was credited correctly, and no suspense account is needed because the trial balance was not affected.

questions.stem_md: Hemant Dairy, an imagined firm, paid an insurance premium of ₹4,000 in cash and debited it to Rent A/c. The effect of this error on net profit is

options.text_md: profit overstated by ₹4,000
profit understated by ₹4,000
no effect, as both are expenses of the same amount
profit overstated by ₹8,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** no effect, as both are expenses of the same amount. Insurance is understated and rent is overstated by the same ₹4,000, and both are charged against profit, so total expenses and net profit are unchanged. The profit would change only if the wrong account were a capital item.

questions.stem_md: Jyoti Stores, an imagined firm, bought a delivery van for ₹60,000 by cheque and debited the amount to Repairs A/c. The effect on net profit is that it is

options.text_md: overstated by ₹60,000
not affected
understated by ₹60,000
understated by ₹1,20,000

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** understated by ₹60,000. The van is a capital item, but its cost was charged to Repairs, an expense, so expenses are too high by ₹60,000 and the profit is too low by the same amount. Overstatement would need the opposite mistake, and the amount is not doubled.

questions.stem_md: Repairs of ₹7,500 on an old machine of Kunal Press, an imagined firm, were paid in cash and debited to Machinery A/c. The effect on net profit is that it is

options.text_md: overstated by ₹7,500
understated by ₹7,500
not affected
not affected, because the trial balance still agrees

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** overstated by ₹7,500. Repairs are a revenue expense, and by debiting the machine the expense is left out of the profit and loss account, so profit is too high by ₹7,500. Agreement of the trial balance says nothing about profit.

questions.stem_md: An audit of Pranav Traders, an imagined firm, finds that its trial balance agrees although Purchases A/c is overcast by ₹3,200. Which second error, with this one, explains why the trial balance still agrees?

options.text_md: Sales A/c undercast by ₹3,200
Wages A/c overcast by ₹3,200
Discount Allowed A/c overcast by ₹3,200
Sales A/c overcast by ₹3,200

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Sales A/c overcast by ₹3,200. Overcast Purchases adds ₹3,200 to the debit side, so another error must add ₹3,200 to the credit side or remove it from the debit side. Overcast Sales adds ₹3,200 to the credit side and cancels it. An undercast Sales account, and overcast Wages or Discount Allowed, would each widen the gap to ₹6,400.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Rekha Mills, an imagined firm, had been agreed by opening a Suspense A/c with a credit balance of ₹5,000. When the first error was rectified, Suspense A/c was debited ₹3,200, leaving a credit balance of ₹1,800. This balance shows that

options.text_md: all errors have been found, and ₹1,800 is profit
other one-sided errors, with a net effect of ₹1,800 on the debit side, are still to be found
the trial balance disagrees by ₹1,800
the first error was rectified wrongly

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** other one-sided errors, with a net effect of ₹1,800 on the debit side, are still to be found. A credit balance in the suspense account means the debit side of the books is still ₹1,800 too high, and the account closes only when errors with that net effect have been found. The trial balance still agrees because the suspense balance is part of it, and nothing suggests the first rectification was wrong.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the trial balance of Dilip Optics, an imagined firm, agrees, its books are free from errors.

**Reason (R):** Errors of principle and compensating errors do not disturb the agreement of the trial balance.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The assertion is false because some errors do not change either column. The reason is true, but it shows why the assertion fails rather than supporting it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A suspense account is opened only when a trial balance has already been prepared and does not agree.

**Reason (R):** Errors found before the trial balance is prepared are corrected directly in the accounts or by journal entries, so no difference arises.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. A difference exists only after a trial balance has been drawn up, and errors corrected earlier leave nothing to carry to a suspense account, which explains the assertion.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A credit sale left out of every book of Hari Traders, an imagined firm, does not stop its trial balance from agreeing.

**Reason (R):** When a transaction is left out completely, the debit and the credit are both missing, so the columns stay equal.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true. Both aspects are missing, so debits still equal credits, and this is exactly why the assertion holds.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Debiting Purchases A/c with the cost of a machine bought for cash is an error of principle.

**Reason (R):** This error makes the debit column of the trial balance exceed the credit column.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The assertion is true because a capital item is treated as a revenue item. The reason is false: the same amount is debited and credited, so the trial balance still agrees.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Crediting commission received of ₹5,400 to Rent A/c does not change the net profit of Isha Studio, an imagined firm.

**Reason (R):** Commission received is an income and rent is an expense.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both are true, but the reason does not explain the assertion. Profit is unchanged because the income is understated and the expense is understated by equal amounts, and they cancel. The nature of the two accounts alone would not guarantee that.

questions.stem_md: True or false: if the trial balance of an imagined firm agrees, the ledger accounts are certainly free from errors.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** An agreed trial balance shows only that debits equal credits in total; errors of omission, principle, wrong accounts and compensating errors can all remain.

questions.stem_md: True or false: after every error has been rectified, a suspense account remains in the books as a permanent account with its balance.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The suspense account is temporary. It is closed when the errors are rectified, and a balance left would mean errors still lie undiscovered.

questions.stem_md: True or false: a two-sided error found before the trial balance is prepared is rectified by a journal entry.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** A two-sided error affects two accounts, and the correction is made through a journal entry that debits and credits the accounts concerned.

questions.stem_md: When a trial balance does not agree, the difference is placed in a ___ account; when all errors are rectified its balance becomes ___.
questions.solution_md: The difference goes to the suspense account, and each rectification reduces it until the balance is nil.

questions.stem_md: The three methods of preparing a trial balance are the ___ method, the totals method and the ___ method.
questions.solution_md: They are the balances method, the totals method and the totals and balances method.

questions.stem_md: Match each error of an imagined firm in column A with its type in column B.

options.text_md: Goods bought on credit for ₹800 never entered in any book
A paint bill for repainting the office debited to Building A/c
A receipt from Rohit Sen credited to the account of Rohan Sethi
Sales book and purchases book each overcast by ₹1,000

Repainting is a revenue expense, so debiting it to the building account is an error of principle. A posting to the wrong person is a commission. Two overcastings of equal amount on opposite sides cancel and are compensating errors.

Total both sides of each ledger account and find its balance
List each balance in the debit column or the credit column according to its side
Post all journal entries to the ledger accounts

Search for the errors and rectify each through a journal entry
Place the difference in the Suspense A/c so that the totals agree
Total the two columns and find the difference

questions.stem_md: Leela Crafts, an imagined firm, prepared its trial balance on 31 March 2028 with these balances: Cash ₹15,000, Debtors ₹45,000, Opening stock ₹60,000, Furniture ₹30,000, Purchases ₹2,10,000, Rent ₹18,000, Creditors ₹40,000, Sales ₹2,60,000. The only account missing from the list is Capital A/c, and the trial balance agrees once it is included. Find the balance of Capital A/c (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: The debit balances total 3,78,000. The listed credit balances (creditors and sales) total 3,00,000. For the columns to agree, Capital A/c must be a credit balance of 3,78,000 − 3,00,000 = ₹78,000.

questions.stem_md: Ishan Brothers, an imagined firm, has these ledger balances on 31 March 2028: Cash ₹22,000, Capital ₹1,50,000, Debtors ₹38,000, Creditors ₹26,000, Purchases ₹1,20,000, Sales ₹1,64,000, Rent ₹9,000, Drawings ₹15,000, Furniture ₹1,36,000. Find the total of the debit column of its trial balance (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Debit balances: cash, debtors, purchases, rent, drawings and furniture, which total 22,000 + 38,000 + 1,20,000 + 9,000 + 15,000 + 1,36,000 = ₹3,40,000. Capital, creditors and sales are credit balances, and they total the same ₹3,40,000.

questions.stem_md: The ledger balances of Dev Pharma, an imagined firm, are debit: Cash ₹45,000, Debtors ₹1,12,000, Purchases ₹64,000, Drawings ₹28,500; credit: Capital ₹1,35,000, Sales ₹78,000, Creditors ₹31,000. The accountant lists them in a trial balance and places the difference in a Suspense A/c so that the columns agree. Find the amount of the Suspense A/c (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Debit column = 2,49,500; credit column = 2,44,000. The debit column is larger by ₹5,500, so the Suspense A/c is credited with ₹5,500.

questions.stem_md: Sai Traders, an imagined firm, finds that its trial balance does not agree. Two errors are traced: the sales book was undercast by ₹3,500, and rent of ₹2,700 paid in cash was posted to Rent A/c as ₹4,500. Both errors affect only one side. What amount was carried to the Suspense A/c to agree the trial balance (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Undercast Sales leaves the credit side short by 3,500. The excess rent debit adds 1,800 to the debit side. Net, the debit side is higher by 3,500 + 1,800 = ₹5,300, so the Suspense A/c was credited with ₹5,300.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Sandeep Cycles, an imagined firm, agreed only after a Suspense A/c was opened with a debit balance of ₹5,000. Three errors were later traced: (i) the sales book overcast by ₹4,500; (ii) rent of ₹3,200 posted to Rent A/c as ₹5,000; (iii) discount received of ₹1,200 posted to Discount Received A/c as ₹3,500. After errors (i) and (ii) alone are rectified, what debit balance is left in the Suspense A/c (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md:
| Dr: Particulars | ₹ | Cr: Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Difference in trial balance | 5,000 | By Sales A/c | 4,500 |
| To Rent A/c | 1,800 | By Balance c/d | 2,300 |
|  | **6,800** |  | **6,800** |

Opening debit 5,000; error (i) credits the account with 4,500; error (ii) debits it with 1,800. Balance = 5,000 − 4,500 + 1,800 = ₹2,300 (debit), which is exactly what error (iii) will clear.

questions.stem_md: Chhaya Boutique, an imagined shop, has these ledger balances before its trial balance is prepared. Debit: Cash ₹12,000, Cash at bank ₹64,000, Rohit Sen ₹31,000, Opening stock ₹55,000, Furniture ₹30,000, Purchases ₹2,58,000, Wages ₹22,000, Rent ₹14,100, Drawings ₹20,000. Credit: Capital ₹2,38,000, Verma Traders ₹58,000, Sales ₹2,03,700, Commission received ₹10,000. The following errors are then found: (i) a computer bought for ₹18,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c; (ii) a credit sale of ₹7,000 to Rohit Sen was omitted from all books; (iii) rent of ₹6,500 paid in cash was posted to Rent A/c as ₹5,600; (iv) the sales book was overcast by ₹2,700. Find the total of the debit column of the trial balance prepared after all four errors are rectified (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: Debit total before rectification = 5,06,100. Error (i) moves 18,000 between two debit accounts and does not change the total. Error (ii) adds 7,000 to the debtor and 7,000 to Sales, so each column rises by 7,000. Error (iii) adds 900 to Rent A/c, a debit. Error (iv) lowers Sales, a credit, by 2,700. Debit total = 5,06,100 + 7,000 + 900 = ₹5,14,000; the credit total, 5,09,700 + 7,000 − 2,700, is the same ₹5,14,000.

questions.stem_md: Maya Optical, an imagined shop, reported a net profit of ₹85,000 for the year ended 31 March 2028. Later these errors were found: (i) the purchases book was overcast by ₹5,000; (ii) a credit sale of ₹12,000 to Lata Iyer was omitted from all books; (iii) a printer bought for ₹9,000 in cash was debited to Repairs A/c; (iv) repairs of ₹4,000 paid in cash were debited to Building A/c. Find the correct net profit (in ₹).
questions.solution_md:
| Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|
| Net profit as per books | 85,000 |
| Add: error 1 (commission) | 5,000 |
| Add: error 2 (omission) | 12,000 |
| Add: error 3 (principle) | 9,000 |
| Less: error 4 (principle) | −4,000 |
| **Corrected net profit** | **1,07,000** |

Errors (i), (ii) and (iii) understated the profit by 5,000, 12,000 and 9,000; error (iv) overstated it by 4,000. Corrected profit = 85,000 + 26,000 − 4,000 = ₹1,07,000.

questions.stem_md: The books of Jai Hardware, an imagined firm, contain three errors: (i) the sales book was overcast by ₹8,000; (ii) furniture bought for ₹20,000 by cheque was debited to Purchases A/c; (iii) wages of ₹2,500 paid in cash were debited to Salaries A/c. By how much is the net profit shown by the books understated, taking all three errors together (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md: Error (i) overstates profit by 8,000. Error (ii) overcharges Purchases and understates profit by 20,000. Error (iii) moves an expense between two expense accounts, so profit is unchanged. Net effect = 20,000 − 8,000 = ₹12,000 understated.

questions.stem_md: Falguni Textiles, an imagined firm, sold goods to Manoj Pandey on credit. He returned goods worth ₹2,100, which were debited correctly to Sales Returns A/c but credited to his account as ₹1,200. His account in the ledger shows a debit balance of ₹14,700. Find the correct balance of his account (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: His account was credited 2,100 − 1,200 = 900 too little, so its debit balance is 900 too high. Correct balance = 14,700 − 900 = ₹13,800 (debit).

questions.stem_md: After its trial balance was agreed with the help of a Suspense A/c, Tarun Traders, an imagined firm, traced three errors: (i) a discount allowed of ₹1,200 to Lata Iyer was credited to her account but not debited to Discount Allowed A/c; (ii) a credit sale of ₹6,400 to Kamal Arora was debited to his account as ₹4,600, with Sales A/c credited correctly; (iii) postage of ₹3,000 paid in cash was debited to Telephone A/c. Find the total of the debit column of the journal entries that rectify the three errors (in ₹).
questions.solution_md:
| Particulars | Dr (₹) | Cr (₹) |
|---|---|---|
| Discount Allowed A/c Dr. | 1,200 |  |
| To Suspense A/c |  | 1,200 |
| *(Being discount allowed not posted to Discount Allowed A/c)* |  |  |
| Kamal Arora A/c Dr. | 1,800 |  |
| To Suspense A/c |  | 1,800 |
| *(Being sale debited to Kamal Arora short)* |  |  |

| To Telephone A/c |  | 3,000 |

Debits: 1,200 + 1,800 + 3,000 = ₹6,000. Entries (i) and (ii) carry the Suspense A/c as the other side; entry (iii) is a plain journal entry.

questions.stem_md: The trial balance of Raghav Mills, an imagined firm, shows a debit column total of ₹4,56,200 and a credit column total of ₹4,59,800. The accountant discovers that a single debit balance was wrongly written in the credit column and nothing else is wrong. Find the amount of that balance (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: A debit balance entered as a credit lowers the debit column by the balance and raises the credit column by the same amount, so the gap is twice the balance. Balance = (4,59,800 − 4,56,200) ÷ 2 = 3,600 ÷ 2 = ₹1,800.

questions.stem_md: Define a trial balance.
questions.solution_md: The statement with the date, and its purpose.

answer.model_answer_md: A **trial balance** is a statement that lists the debit balances and the credit balances of all ledger accounts on a given date. It is prepared to check the arithmetical accuracy of posting and balancing.

marking_scheme.step: A statement of debit and credit balances of ledger accounts on a date

questions.stem_md: State any two objectives of preparing a trial balance.
questions.solution_md: Any two objectives, each stated and explained briefly.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **To check arithmetical accuracy:** equal columns show that posting and balancing are arithmetically sound.
2. **To summarise the ledger:** it brings the balances of all accounts together, and supplies the figures for the financial statements.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why an agreed trial balance does not prove that the books of Gauri Gifts, an imagined firm, are free from errors.
questions.solution_md: Errors that leave the totals unchanged, and compensating errors.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Some errors, such as a complete omission, an error of principle or a posting to a wrong account of the same kind, put equal amounts on both sides, so the totals still agree.
2. Compensating errors cancel each other, so the totals agree although the accounts are wrong.

questions.stem_md: Name the three methods of preparing a trial balance. Which of them lists only the closing balances?
questions.solution_md: Three methods named, then the one that lists closing balances.

answer.model_answer_md: The three methods are the **balances method**, the **totals method** and the **totals and balances method**. The balances method lists only the closing balance of each ledger account.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between an error of commission and an error of omission, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: The difference with one example for each.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Commission:** a transaction is recorded but posted wrongly, for example ₹3,000 received from one debtor credited to another debtor.

questions.stem_md: Explain the four types of errors in accounting, giving one example of each from the books of an imagined firm.
questions.solution_md: Each type with its meaning and an example.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Errors of commission:** a transaction is recorded but posted wrongly, in amount, side or account, or totalled, balanced or carried forward wrongly; for example ₹2,000 received from one debtor is credited to another.
2. **Errors of omission:** a transaction is left out completely or only one side of it is posted; for example a credit sale is not entered in any book.
3. **Errors of principle:** a capital item is treated as revenue, or the reverse; for example a machine is debited to Purchases A/c.
4. **Compensating errors:** errors whose effects cancel; for example Sales and Purchases are both overcast by ₹1,000.

answer.model_answer_md: The statement is **not correct**. An agreed trial balance proves only arithmetical accuracy: the debit balances equal the credit balances. It cannot reveal errors that put equal amounts on both sides, such as a complete omission of a transaction, an error of principle, a posting to a wrong account of the same kind, or a wrong amount written on both sides. Compensating errors also cancel. The books may therefore still be wrong, and profit and the balance sheet may be misstated. The trial balance is a useful first check, but it cannot replace a review of the accounts.
